question_details.description:
The [International Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice) was established, as part of the United Nations, in 1945. It is the only international court that resolves disputes between states. States however [must consent](https://auilr.org/2025/10/03/heads-i-win-tails-you-lose-how-irans-opinio-juris-claim-of-sovereign-immunity-highlights-a-crisis-of-authority-for-the-international-court-of-justice/) to its jurisdiction and enforcement of its orders are subject to veto by the [UN Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council), which significantly limits its influence and power.

Nonetheless, many states have had occasion to seek relief from the ICJ over the years. Since the [first case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corfu_Channel_case) was opened in 1947, [201 (contentious) cases](https://www.icj-cij.org/contentious-cases?dateorder=introduction\&order=desc) have been brought before the ICJ, including five cases already brought during 2025 (by Sudan, Iran, France, Lithuania, and Russia).

**80 Years of the UN: Security Council Reform Is Imperative**
The United Nations (UN) marked its 80th anniversary in October 2025, but its ability to resolve international conflicts has significantly declined, necessitating urgent reform. Established in 1945 after two world wars, the UN was designed to maintain peace, with initial membership of 51 countries growing to 193 today; Japan joined in 1956 following the San Francisco Peace Treaty. However, the Security Council—the UN’s central body—has suffered functional failure, particularly due to Russia’s abandonment of its responsibilities by invading Ukraine. The Security Council’s permanent members (the U.S., UK, France, China, and Russia) hold veto power, meaning any single country can block a resolution. Despite the UN’s membership expanding to nearly four times its original size, the Security Council remains at 15 members, including five permanent members. The U.S., a founding force behind the UN, has shown little leadership in reform; former President Trump criticized the UN in September 2025, calling it a source of problems and reducing financial contributions. Analysts warn that Al-Hishari’s case may be the first of a broader ICC campaign targeting figures across Libya, potentially deepening internal divisions if not managed with legal and political balance.
